To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

youth-oriented civic Web sites tend to promote a model of citizenship that emphasizes dutiful participation and a passive, uncritical consumption of media, while the Web sphere is also populated by a growing number of youth Web sites that promote a model of expressive citizenship that emphasizes active, participatory media creation and peer content sharing.

the youth Web sphere reflects the tension between the traditional model of citizenship, which is characterized by the one-way communication of information from authorities to citizens, and the new model of citizenship, characterized by the two-way communication between citizens.
youth civic engagement is increasingly mediated by the Internet and social media and that the Web sites of civic organizations are often out of step with these changes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways that civic engagement is promoted and communicated in the youth Web sphere.
the question of whether the Web is a medium that is well suited to promoting civic engagement, or whether it is more a reflection of the changing nature of citizenship itself.
the following question: How do youth Web sites communicate civic engagement?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the youth Web sphere is a complex and dynamic arena for the development of civic skills and citizenship.
the youth of today are becoming more expressive and less dutiful.
the current youth Web sphere does not represent a cohesive, unified model of citizenship.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the youth civic Web sphere has become a complex space of civic expression, where youth are using social media and other Web 2.0 tools to engage with civic issues, but that the organizations operating in that space have not yet caught up with the new forms and styles of civic engagement that youth are developing.
youth are increasingly using social media as a way to express themselves and to share content with peers.
the youth Web sites we examined were not very effective in promoting youth engagement in the public sphere.
The main takeaway from our work is that
youth civic Web sites need to be more responsive to the expressive, participatory, and social media styles of the younger generation.
civic organizations need to be more aware of and responsive to the evolving civic styles and practices of the young people they serve.
youth-oriented organizations need to rethink their communication strategies and the skills they teach if they are to remain relevant to the new generation of civic activists and citizens.
